meta.title: EFU Life HOD Situational Judgment Assessment

Developing: Demonstrates limited ownership in contributing to functional and enterprise priorities
Struggles to navigate ambiguity, resistance, or group dynamics across contexts
Shows minimal ability to influence alignment or contribute to outcomes across pillars
Remains task-focused with limited connection to strategic priorities or broader impact
Requires direction; limited evidence of readiness for higher-level responsibility
Proficient: Contributes to functional priorities, though alignment to enterprise priorities is inconsistent
Participates in discussions and decisions but may not consistently drive clarity or direction
Demonstrates basic ability to collaborate and support outcomes across pillars
Handles ambiguity and resistance with some structure, though often reactively
Impact is primarily within own scope, with limited influence beyond immediate context
Advanced: Proactively contributes to functional and enterprise priorities, with clear linkage to outcomes
Demonstrates structured thinking in navigating ambiguity, trade-offs and group dynamics
Actively drives alignment, decision-making and outcomes across multiple pillars
Balances short-term delivery with emerging strategic considerations
Influences others effectively within and across functions to achieve aligned outcomes
Role Model: Consistently operates with an enterprise-first mindset, shaping direction aligned to strategic priorities
Navigates complexity, ambiguity, and resistance with clarity, judgment, and composure
Drives alignment and outcomes across all pillars, influencing beyond immediate function
Integrates strategy, execution, collaboration and people impact seamlessly
Anticipates future needs and reframes challenges to strengthen enterprise outcomes

items.scenario: The CEO has flagged a concern about EFU Life's slowing growth in the 35–45 age segment. You head a core function (e.g. Operations, Actuarial, or Marketing). In the next ExCo meeting, the item on segment strategy is open for discussion.

options.text: Come prepared with a view on what's driving the slowdown and how your function could contribute to a response, even outside your usual remit.
Contribute only when asked about your function's specific role, since segment strategy sits primarily with Sales and Marketing.
Propose an enterprise-wide perspective on the segment, including implications for product design, distribution, servicing, and risk — and advocate for coordinated ownership.
Share what your function can do to support whichever segment strategy is adopted by the business owners.

items.scenario: A new entrant is aggressively acquiring market share in takaful through a partnership model EFU Life has not prioritized. Your function is asked for input at a planning session.

options.text: Reframe the conversation around what the competitor's success reveals about the market, and shape an enterprise-level response with peers.
Explain how your function would support a response if leadership decides to pursue one.
Offer a point of view on whether and how EFU Life should respond, based on your function's vantage point.
Share what your function is currently doing; the competitive response is a business decision.

items.scenario: Your team has inherited a long list of carry-over initiatives from the previous year, plus three new strategic priorities from the CEO. Capacity is clearly insufficient for all of them.

options.text: Work through the full list; flag resourcing concerns if things slip.
Identify which carry-over initiatives to stop or defer, communicate the decisions, and refocus the team.
Negotiate for additional resources to deliver the expanded agenda.
Redefine the function's 12–18 month agenda around the new priorities, retire what no longer fits, and align the team's operating rhythm to it.

items.scenario: A team member proposes a well-intentioned improvement project that is legitimate but does not align with your top priorities for the year.

options.text: Explain why it does not fit this year's priorities and decline it, while acknowledging the thinking.
Use the conversation to re-anchor the team on the priorities and help the person redirect their energy to something on-strategy.
Approve it; good initiatives should not be discouraged.
Approve it with a caveat that top priorities must not be affected.

items.scenario: You are reviewing Q2 progress on strategic initiatives. One major workstream is at 40% of plan, another is on track, and a third is ahead.

options.text: Reallocate time, attention, and possibly resources across the three based on their strategic value and risk.
Ask each workstream lead to explain their status and present a recovery plan for the one behind.
Use the review to recalibrate the portfolio overall — stopping, accelerating, or resourcing workstreams based on changed conditions.
Focus your intervention on the workstream that is behind.

items.scenario: Your strategy requires two critical new capabilities. Neither exists in-house. Budget allows for one new hire or one external partner, not both.

options.text: Choose the option most likely to deliver a visible win this year.
Choose based on which capability creates longer-term functional advantage, even if slower to show results.
Defer the decision until more budget becomes available.
Design a phased plan that sequences both capabilities, using creative sourcing and reallocation to accelerate the second.

items.scenario: Claim processing times have been inconsistent for the last two quarters. Some cases close in 48 hours; others take three weeks. Customer complaints are rising.

options.text: Instruct the team to accelerate pending cases and escalate exceptions to you.
Redesign processing as a predictable system with clear ownership, SLAs by case type, and self-correcting controls — so performance does not require your intervention.
Reinforce the existing SOP with the team and tighten monitoring.
Map the current process end-to-end, identify the bottlenecks, and redesign the flow.

items.scenario: A key process in your function depends heavily on one senior staff member. They have performed reliably for years but are now considering retirement.

options.text: Document the process, reduce single-person dependency, and cross-train multiple people.
Ask them to delay retirement until a successor is identified.
Start grooming a replacement to take over the role in time.
Use this as a trigger to audit all key-person dependencies across the function and systemically reduce them.

items.scenario: A new service standard has been announced. Three months in, you notice adherence is 78% while the target is 95%.

options.text: Remind the team of the target and monitor compliance.
Use leading indicators in the process to catch issues before they become non-compliance.
Embed the standard into the operating system so that meeting it is the default, not an act of compliance.
Investigate the reasons for non-adherence and address the top causes.

items.scenario: You have both a leading indicator (submission quality) and a lagging indicator (turnaround time). Leading is declining; lagging is still within SLA.

options.text: Use the pattern to strengthen early-warning mechanisms across other processes in the function.
Act on the leading indicator now to prevent future SLA breaches.
Continue current focus since the SLA is still met.
Flag the leading indicator in the monthly review so the team is aware.

items.scenario: Your function's headcount has grown 18% in three years; output has grown 12%.

options.text: Freeze hiring until output catches up with headcount.
Justify the gap by citing increased complexity and regulatory demands.
Identify which activities have grown disproportionately and examine whether automation or redesign could reduce effort.
Take a zero-based view of roles and activities, and restructure the function around current strategic priorities.

items.scenario: You identify savings worth PKR 25 million from a process redesign. The CFO suggests returning the savings to the bottom line.

options.text: Return the savings; a cost saving is a cost saving.
Make a structured case for reallocating the savings to strategic priorities, with expected returns quantified.
Propose reinvesting part of the savings in capability-building that will compound over time.
Return most of the savings and retain a small amount for team rewards.

items.scenario: Your internal audit has raised three findings in your function. Two are procedural; one points to a potential control gap that has not caused an incident yet.

options.text: Use the findings to upgrade the function's overall control environment, including preventive controls for risks that have not yet materialized.
Close the two procedural findings quickly to demonstrate responsiveness.
Close all three by the due date.
Close the findings and examine whether similar control gaps may exist elsewhere in the function.

items.scenario: A senior leader from another function asks you to approve an exception to a control in your area to meet a quarter-end target.

options.text: Decline but offer to escalate to the CRO for a formal exception.
Decline, explain the risk rationale clearly, and offer an alternative path that meets the target without breaching the control.
Decline, and use the incident to examine whether target-setting is unintentionally creating pressure to compromise controls across the enterprise.
Decline the request and stay out of the discussion.

items.scenario: Bancassurance has been your main growth channel for a decade. Early signals suggest digital direct-to-customer models may disrupt this.

options.text: Lead a cross-functional re-examination of EFU Life's distribution strategy for the next decade.
Pilot a direct-to-customer capability while protecting the bancassurance business.
Monitor the digital direct-to-customer trend while continuing to invest in bancassurance.
Continue optimizing the current bancassurance channel given its proven performance.

items.scenario: You are asked, 'What in your function today will not work in three years?' You are expected to answer in the next ExCo meeting.

options.text: Identify two or three specific activities that are vulnerable and explain why.
Decline to speculate; three years is too far out to predict.
Present a clear view of the function's vulnerabilities, with a plan in place to address each, sequenced by urgency.
List processes that are already showing signs of strain.

items.scenario: Your function relies heavily on a legacy system that works but limits flexibility. A new platform is available but would require 9–12 months of disruption to implement.

options.text: Wait for IT to propose a migration plan.
Lead a business case for modernization grounded in strategic value, not just system replacement.
Continue with the legacy system since it is functional.
Partner with IT to build a phased migration plan that manages the disruption.

items.scenario: A peer function has achieved 60% straight-through processing through automation. Your function is at 15%.

options.text: Note the benchmark; your function has different complexity.
Develop a roadmap to close the gap, with clear targets and milestones.
Meet with the peer to understand their approach.
Set an aspirational STP target for your function and redesign workflows to achieve it, using the peer function's experience as one input among several.

items.scenario: A team member proposes testing a small change to the customer onboarding flow. The business case is uncertain but the cost of testing is low.

options.text: Approve the test if it does not interfere with current operations.
Ask for a more detailed business case before approving.
Use the proposal to build a structured experimentation pipeline the function can run continuously.
Approve the test with clear success metrics and a defined learning window.

items.scenario: Your annual improvement program has delivered incremental gains but no step-change. Leadership asks why.

options.text: Shift the model from periodic improvement programs to embedded continuous experimentation in daily work.
Explain that current performance levels leave little room for step-change.
Examine whether the improvement approach itself is constraining outcomes and redesign it.
Commit to setting more ambitious improvement targets next year.

items.scenario: A peer HOD has publicly criticized your function in an ExCo meeting. The criticism has some truth to it but was delivered without prior notice.

options.text: Acknowledge the valid points publicly and follow up with the peer directly to understand the concern.
Ask the CEO for a private conversation to clarify facts afterward.
Treat the situation as a signal that the peer relationship needs investment, and rebuild the partnership proactively.
Respond defensively in the meeting to protect the function's reputation.

items.scenario: A new HOD has joined a peer function. You have not yet met them.

options.text: Engage when a business need arises that involves their function.
Build a sustained partnership from day one, including shared rituals for ongoing alignment.
Send a welcome note and offer a meeting when convenient.
Proactively schedule a working conversation to understand their priorities and share yours.

items.scenario: A customer experience initiative requires contributions from five functions. Progress has stalled because ownership is unclear.

options.text: Treat the stall as a signal that the enterprise lacks a model for cross-functional outcomes and advocate for one.
Propose that your function lead the initiative.
Deliver your piece well and let leadership resolve ownership.
Work with peers to clarify ownership, shared KPIs, and governance, then move forward.

items.scenario: Your function is asked to contribute to an enterprise initiative that will benefit EFU Life but offers no direct credit to your function.

options.text: Contribute actively because the enterprise outcome matters, regardless of credit.
Contribute the minimum required and focus on your function's own priorities.
Contribute what is asked without prioritizing it above your own agenda.
Advocate for the initiative, help design shared measures of success, and bring peers along.

items.scenario: In an ExCo meeting, you disagree with a decision that is about to be finalized. Others are ready to move on.

options.text: Stay silent to avoid slowing the meeting and raise concerns later.
State your disagreement clearly, offer your reasoning, and let the group decide.
Ensure the disagreement is fully heard and resolved before commitment, so that alignment is real, not compliant.
Note your concern briefly for the minutes and go along with the decision.

items.scenario: Two of your team members have been in sustained conflict over responsibilities on a shared project. Work is being affected.

options.text: Use the situation to examine whether the role design itself is creating the conflict and address root causes.
Facilitate a direct conversation between them to resolve the underlying issue.
Reassign one of them to reduce friction.
Meet with each separately to hear their perspective.

items.scenario: You are asked to name a successor for your role. Realistically, no one on your team is ready today.

options.text: Name the most tenured team member as a provisional successor.
State that no internal successor is currently available.
Identify the strongest candidate, define a development plan, and work it actively.
Build multiple successor pipelines from within and outside the team, with deliberate development and cross-exposure.

items.scenario: A strong performer on your team has been approached for a role in another function. You need them in your function.

options.text: Make the case for retaining them in their current role.
Actively encourage the move and use it as a signal of your commitment to enterprise talent development.
Support the move as a development opportunity, while planning for the gap.
Agree reluctantly if leadership supports the move.

items.scenario: At year-end calibration, you are asked to differentiate ratings across your team. Most of your team delivered well; differentiation feels arbitrary.

options.text: Differentiate slightly to meet calibration guidelines.
Differentiate meaningfully based on actual impact, even if conversations will be hard.
Use the calibration to strengthen how performance is discussed and measured throughout the year, not just at year-end.
Rate the team uniformly to reflect shared effort.

items.scenario: You are away for two weeks. On return, you find that performance slipped in your absence on issues the team should have been able to handle.

options.text: Increase oversight and reduce future absences when possible.
Clarify decision rights and expectations with the team.
Redesign the function so that performance is sustained by systems and accountability, not by your presence.
Identify why the team could not act and build the capability and authority needed.

items.scenario: Your engagement score has dropped from 82 to 74 over two survey cycles. The rest of EFU Life is stable.

options.text: Treat the decline as a signal to examine the function's culture and leadership approach systemically.
Hold open conversations with the team to surface concerns and act visibly on them.
Investigate which specific dimensions have dropped and address them.
Question the validity of the survey methodology.

items.scenario: A team member raises, in confidence, concerns about inclusion in team decisions. Others have not raised similar concerns.

options.text: Examine team decision-making patterns honestly and make changes.
Thank them and suggest they raise it through formal channels.
Treat the feedback as a signal to invest in inclusion as a deliberate leadership practice.
Take note of the feedback and be more mindful going forward.

items.scenario: In your 360 feedback, multiple respondents note that you interrupt others in meetings. You were not aware of this.

options.text: Use the feedback as a trigger for a broader examination of how your leadership impacts others.
Make an effort to be mindful in meetings going forward.
Acknowledge the pattern openly, seek specific examples, and work on it deliberately.
Consider the context; interruptions sometimes help move decisions.

items.scenario: Under heavy pressure last quarter, your directness came across to the team as harsh. You had not noticed.

options.text: Recognize that pressure affects everyone and move on.
Examine what triggers the shift and work on responding differently under pressure.
Apologize to the team and try to manage tone better.
Treat the feedback as fundamental, not cosmetic, and invest in sustained change including coaching if helpful.
